title: 10. Security & Auth: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
summary: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) is an attack where a malicious script is injected into a trusted website and executed in the browser of another user, allowing the attacker to steal session tokens, hijack accounts, deface content,…
objectives: What are the three types of XSS, and how do they differ?
What is output encoding and why must it be context-aware?
What is Content Security Policy (CSP) and how does it mitigate XSS?
Why are HttpOnly cookies important for XSS defense?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) is an attack where a malicious script is injected into a trusted website and executed in the browser of another user, allowing the attacker to steal session tokens, hijack accounts, deface content, or pivot to broader exploitation — all within the security context of the vulnerable site.

XSS is arguably the most consequential web vulnerability in the history of the internet. It exploits a fundamental tension: web pages are made of HTML, which can include `<script>` tags that execute JavaScript, and modern web apps routinely render user-supplied content (comments, profile bios, search queries, chat messages, file names). If the application takes user input and writes it into the HTML response without escaping special characters, then any input containing `<script>alert(1)</script>` becomes executable JavaScript in every visitor's browser. The script runs in the origin of the vulnerable site, so it can read cookies (if not HttpOnly), make authenticated API calls, modify the DOM, capture keystrokes, and exfiltrate data to the attacker's server. The same-origin policy, normally the browser's main defense, becomes the attacker's weapon: the script's origin is the victim site, so it has the full privileges of the victim's session on that site. OWASP has listed XSS in the Top 10 since 2003; despite decades of awareness, it remains in the 2021 list at #3 (under "Injection") because new frameworks, new patterns, and new developers keep reintroducing it.

XSS comes in three flavors. **Stored (persistent) XSS** is the most damaging: the attacker's payload is saved on the server (in a database, comment, profile field, chat message) and served to every user who views the page. The classic example is the Samy worm (2005): Samy Kamkar injected a payload into his MySpace profile that, when viewed, added Samy to the viewer's friend list and posted "Samy is my hero" to their profile, then copied itself into their profile. Within 20 hours, it had infected over one million users — making it the fastest-spreading worm in history at the time. MySpace had to shut down to clean up. The payload worked because MySpace allowed HTML in profile bios but tried to filter `<script>` tags — Samy found a bypass using `javascript:` URLs in CSS attributes and innerHTML manipulation. **Reflected (non-persistent) XSS** is more common but less impactful: the payload is included in the victim's request (typically a URL parameter) and reflected back in the response. The victim must be tricked into clicking a malicious link (via phishing, email, social media). The payload is not stored on the server, so each victim must be targeted individually. **DOM-based XSS** is the trickiest: the payload never goes to the server — it's processed entirely in the browser by JavaScript that reads from `location.hash`, `location.search`, `document.referrer`, or other client-side sources and writes to `innerHTML`, `document.write`, `eval`, or other dangerous sinks. The server's response is identical for every request; the vulnerability is in the client-side code.

The mitigations are layered and context-dependent. **Output encoding** is the primary defense: before writing any user-supplied data into HTML, escape the characters that have special meaning (`<`, `>`, `&`, `"`, `'`) to their HTML entity equivalents (`<`, `>`, `&`, `"`, `'`). The encoding must match the context: HTML body context, HTML attribute context (escape quotes), JavaScript context (use `JSON.stringify` with `\uXXXX` escaping for `</script>` and other sequences), URL context (use `encodeURIComponent`), and CSS context (escape backslash and quotes). A common bug is using the wrong encoder for the context — e.g., HTML-encoding data that's then placed inside a JavaScript string, which doesn't prevent `</script>` from breaking out. Modern frameworks (React, Vue, Angular) auto-escape by default; React's JSX, for example, escapes any expression in `{}` unless you explicitly use `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (which should be a code-review red flag). **Content Security Policy (CSP)** is the second layer: a response header that tells the browser which sources of script, style, image, etc. are allowed. A strict CSP (`script-src 'self'`) blocks inline scripts and external script sources the attacker might use, defeating most XSS payloads even if the application has an injection bug. The gold standard is a nonce-based CSP (`script-src 'nonce-abc123' 'strict-dynamic'`) where each response includes a fresh nonce and only scripts with that nonce execute — this allows legitimate inline scripts while blocking attacker-injected ones. CSP does not fix the underlying injection bug, but it dramatically reduces its impact.

**HttpOnly cookies** prevent the script from stealing session cookies via `document.cookie` — the cookie is still sent on requests, but JavaScript cannot read it. This is a critical defense because cookie theft is the most common XSS impact, and it's nearly free (one attribute on the Set-Cookie header). **Cookie prefixes** (`__Host-` and `__Secure-`) add further constraints: `__Host-` requires `Secure`, `Path=/`, no `Domain` attribute, preventing subdomain-based cookie injection. **SameSite cookies** don't directly prevent XSS (the script runs in the same origin), but they limit the impact of session theft by preventing the stolen cookie from being sent on cross-site requests. **Trusted Types** (a W3C draft adopted by Chrome) goes further: it requires all DOM sinks (`innerHTML`, `eval`, `document.write`) to receive a `TrustedHTML` or `TrustedScript` object created by a policy, so a raw string from user input cannot be assigned to a sink — this breaks the DOM-based XSS pattern at the browser level. Google deployed Trusted Types across their internal apps and reduced XSS by ~70%.

The trade-off is security versus developer ergonomics and compatibility. Strict CSP breaks many legacy apps that rely on inline scripts and `eval`; adopting CSP requires either a migration to external scripts + nonces or a phased rollout with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` to identify violations without breaking the page. Trusted Types require refactoring every DOM sink to use a policy, which is a significant migration. React's auto-escaping can be bypassed by `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (legitimate use case: rendering Markdown or rich text), which then requires HTML sanitization (DOMPurify is the gold standard — it parses the HTML, allows a safe subset of tags and attributes, and strips everything else). Sanitization is hard: there have been many DOMPurify mXSS (mutation XSS) bypasses over the years, and rich-text editors that allow complex formatting are a perennial source of bugs. The guidance: prefer plain-text rendering with auto-escaping; if rich text is required, sanitize with a well-maintained library (DOMPurify, sanitize-html), run a strict CSP, and isolate the rendered HTML in a sandboxed iframe so it can't access the parent page's cookies or DOM.

Finally, modern frameworks have shifted the XSS landscape. **Single-page apps** with React/Vue/Angular are largely immune to reflected and stored XSS in templates (auto-escaping) but vulnerable in three places: `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html`, URL fragments written to `href` (a `javascript:` URL is XSS), and template injection in server-side rendering. **Markdown and rich-text rendering** is a major XSS source because users expect formatting but the renderer must allow some HTML. **PostMessage handlers** that accept messages from any origin and write the data to the DOM are a frequent source of DOM XSS. **Web Components** and custom elements that accept HTML attributes can be XSS sinks if they use the attributes in `innerHTML`. The defense-in-depth playbook: framework auto-escaping + strict CSP with nonces + HttpOnly SameSite cookies + DOMPurify for rich text + Trusted Types where supported + Content Security Policy report endpoints to catch violations in production + bug bounty to catch what testing missed. XSS is not solved; it is managed.

options: Output encoding is the practice of converting special characters in user-supplied data to their HTML entity equivalents before writing them into a response, so the browser renders them as…
Trusted Types is a browser API (W3C draft, supported in Chrome) that requires all DOM sinks that can execute scripts or alter the DOM dangerously — innerHTML, outerHTML, document.write,…
CSP is a response header (Content-Security-Policy) that tells the browser which sources of script, style, image, font, frame, and other resources are allowed to load and execute on the page.
The three types are stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS.
quiz.explanation: The three types are stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS. Stored (persistent) XSS is when the attacker's payload is saved on the server (in a database, comment, profile bio, chat message) and served to every user who views the page — it's the most damaging because a single injection can compromise many victims automatically.

quiz.explanation: Output encoding is the practice of converting special characters in user-supplied data to their HTML entity equivalents before writing them into a response, so the browser renders them as visible text rather than interpreting them as HTML or JavaScript. The basic HTML body encoding escapes , &, ", ' to <, >, &, ", '.
